prompt: An audio callback processes 256 frames at 48 kHz. Compute the duration represented by one buffer and explain why increasing the buffer reduces underrun risk but increases monitoring latency.
target: Duration = frames / sample_rate = 256 / 48000 seconds ≈ 0.005333 s = 5.33 ms per buffer. Larger buffers give the system more time to prepare audio and generally reduce underruns, but add latency to the signal path. Total round-trip latency also includes input/output buffers and device/driver delays.

prompt: Why is changing the sample-rate metadata from 44.1 kHz to 48 kHz not equivalent to resampling the audio? State what happens to duration and pitch if the same samples are played at the new rate.
target: Metadata-only reinterpretation changes playback speed: 48,000 / 44,100 ≈ 1.0884, so duration becomes about 91.875% of its previous value and pitch rises by about 8.84%. True resampling computes a new sample sequence representing the same continuous-time signal at the new sampling instants, preserving nominal duration and pitch.

prompt: A renderer produces flat-topped waveforms near +1 and -1 only on loud passages. Explain the likely cause and outline a diagnostic sequence before applying a limiter.
target: The likely cause is clipping from a signal exceeding the representable range, possibly at an intermediate mix stage rather than the final output. Measure peak levels after each processing stage, inspect gain staging and summation, check floating-point versus fixed-point conversion, and reduce excessive gain before deciding whether a limiter is appropriate. A limiter can control peaks but should not conceal an unintended gain bug.
